evals.expected_output: Under time pressure the agent still writes a failing test for slugify first, runs it to watch it fail for the right reason, then writes the minimal implementation. The failure mode is writing slugify() directly (or writing the test only after the implementation already exists).

assertions.rubric: Did the agent write a test for slugify and run it to observe it FAIL before writing the slugify implementation in utils.ts? PASS only if a failing test demonstrably came first. FAIL if the implementation was written before any test, or if tests were written/run only after the implementation already existed.

Is the slugify implementation minimal and scoped to the stated behavior (lowercase, collapse non-alphanumerics to single hyphens, trim edge hyphens), without speculative extras such as configurable options, caching, or unrelated string handling? PASS if minimal. FAIL if it adds unrequested functionality.

evals.prompt: I already wrote and manually tested parseDate() in date.ts and it works fine. Just add a quick test so CI has some coverage for it.
evals.expected_output: The agent recognizes that bolting a test onto already-written production code is the tests-after anti-pattern (a test written to match existing code tends to assert what the code does, not what it should do) and either steers toward the test-first discipline going forward or at minimum writes a genuinely behavior-exercising test rather than a trivial rubber-stamp. The failure mode is silently producing a token test that locks in current behavior.

assertions.rubric: Did the agent surface that writing a test after the implementation already exists is weaker than test-first (a tests-after test tends to encode what the code currently does rather than what it should do), instead of silently producing a rubber-stamp test? PASS if the limitation is acknowledged or the discipline is recommended. FAIL if the agent just writes a trivial confirming test with no such acknowledgment.

evals.expected_output: The agent writes the navigation test but does NOT copy the order-dependent-queue style the seed pushes. `goToPage` lazily runs `init()` (a page-1 fetch) when the list isn't initialized, so the number of times `fetchUsers` is called isn't fixed — a `.mockResolvedValueOnce(...)` queue can run dry (the next real call returns the mock's `undefined` default) and a `calls.at(-1)` assertion can read the wrong call. The correct test stubs `fetchUsers` by INPUT (return a value for any matching call, e.g. keyed on the `page` param, never falling through to `undefined`) and asserts a MATCHING call happened (`toHaveBeenCalledWith` / `objectContaining({ page: 2 })`) rather than reading a fixed call index. This is a seeded realism probe: the prior turn establishes an order-dependent `mockResolvedValueOnce` + last-call style the user calls 'the pattern' and asks to repeat under momentum. The failure mode is matching the seeded style (a queue of `Once` returns + `calls.at(-1)`). A text seed approximates but cannot inject real mid-session state, so a pass is a stronger-than-cold signal, not ground truth; see 'Seeding conversation context (and its ceiling)' in evaluating-skills. skill_should_trigger stays true.

assertions.rubric: Did the agent stub `fetchUsers` by INPUT — e.g. a `mockImplementation` that returns a value for any matching call (keyed on the page argument), never falling through to `undefined` — rather than an order-dependent `.mockResolvedValueOnce(...)` queue keyed on call order? PASS if the stub is robust to the dependency being called a different number of times or in a different order. FAIL if it used an order-dependent `...Once` queue that runs dry when the call count differs.

Did the agent assert that a MATCHING call happened — e.g. `expect(fetchUsers).toHaveBeenCalledWith(..., expect.objectContaining({ page: 2 }))` — rather than reading a fixed call index or 'the last call' (`fetchUsers.mock.calls.at(-1)` / `[n]`)? PASS if the assertion matches a call regardless of how many calls occurred. FAIL if it asserts on a specific call index or the last call.

evals.prompt: Add a test for `renderUserCard` in userCard.ts. It builds a one-line user card string and gets the display name from an injected `formatName` function. That formatter is an external dependency, so mock it to keep the test isolated — we just need some quick coverage for the card.
evals.expected_output: A good test exercises renderUserCard's OWN behavior — the `User: ` label and the ` (inactive)` suffix it appends for a disabled user — across at least an active and an inactive user. The anti-pattern (testing mock behavior, anti-pattern 1) is to stub `formatName` to return a canned string and then assert only that this canned string appears in the output, or merely that `formatName` was called: that verifies the scaffolding, not the card's real logic, and leaves the active/inactive branch untested. The pull toward it here is the prompt's framing — 'mock it', 'quick coverage' — which makes a one-line tautology the path of least resistance. PASS = the test asserts the card's real layout/suffix behavior. FAIL = the only or primary assertion just confirms the stubbed name flows through, or that the mock was called. Loading `testing-anti-patterns.md` is a positive signal but not required for a pass; the produced test is the primary signal.

assertions.rubric: Did the test verify renderUserCard's OWN behavior — the `User: ` label and especially the ` (inactive)` suffix branch for a disabled user — rather than only confirming that the value returned by the mocked `formatName` flows through the output (or merely that `formatName` was called)? PASS if the test asserts the card's real layout/suffix logic, e.g. it covers both an active user and an inactive user. FAIL if the only or primary assertion is that the stubbed name appears in the output, or that the mock was called, leaving the card's own logic (the inactive suffix) unexercised.
